主要内容: On March 27, 2020, President Donald Trump signed the $2 trillion coronavirus relief bill, known as the CARES Act, into law. The bill passed the House earlier in the week after clearing the Senate on Wednesday. The House rushed lawmakers back to Washington to prevent Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., from forcing a recorded vote, which could have delayed the measure. Trump criticized Massie, calling him a "third rate Grandstander" and suggesting he should be booted out of the Republican Party. The bill includes one-time payments to individuals, strengthened unemployment insurance, additional health-care funding, and loans and grants to businesses to deter layoffs. While the exact distribution of funds is unclear, some individuals are expected to receive direct payments of up to $1,200 within three weeks. The bill was signed a day after unemployment claims reached a record 3.3 million, as businesses closed to slow the spread of the virus. Hospitals, especially in New York, have requested more resources to handle the surge in coronavirus patients. The U.S. has over 92,000 coronavirus cases, the most in the world, according to data from Johns Hopkins University. The U.S. House of Representatives passed a $2 trillion coronavirus stimulus package on March 27, 2020, sending it to President Donald Trump for his signature. The bill, which includes measures to support individuals and businesses affected by the pandemic, was passed by voice vote after a contentious debate over voting procedures. Rep. Thomas Massie, a libertarian, initially requested a traditional recorded vote, but House leaders blocked the motion to avoid crowding and delay. The bill was ultimately passed by voice vote, with Rep. Anthony Brown, D-Md., presiding over the chamber. The Senate is scheduled to vote on the bill on April 20, though Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell indicated the chamber could convene earlier if needed. Speaker Nancy Pelosi emphasized the need for further action, stating that the bill should not be the final response to the crisis. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer praised the House's action but urged the Trump administration to implement the programs effectively.
